stem:
A 33-year-old woman skips breakfast and lunch for a medical procedure. By late afternoon her blood glucose begins to fall, and her pancreas responds to keep glucose available for her brain.

Which of the following best describes this response?

options.label: A
options.text: Delta cells release somatostatin, blocking all islet hormone output
options.misconception: An inhibitory islet hormone is being cast as the fasting responder.
options.explanation: Somatostatin inhibits both glucagon and insulin release; the fasting response is alpha-cell glucagon stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis to raise blood glucose.

options.label: B
options.text: Beta cells release insulin, driving glucose into skeletal muscle
options.misconception: The fed-state hormone is being assigned to the fasting state.
options.explanation: Insulin from beta cells lowers blood glucose by driving uptake into muscle and fat — the opposite of what fasting requires; falling glucose suppresses insulin and triggers glucagon instead.

options.label: C
options.text: Alpha cells release glucagon, driving hepatic glycogen breakdown into glucose
options.misconception: None; falling glucose triggers alpha-cell glucagon, which halts glycogen synthesis and stimulates glycogen breakdown in the liver.
options.explanation: Low blood glucose stimulates glucagon release from pancreatic alpha cells; glucagon turns off hepatic glycogen synthesis and stimulates glycogen breakdown, releasing glucose into the bloodstream.

options.label: D
options.text: The liver releases its stored insulin into the portal vein
options.misconception: The liver is being assigned a hormone it neither makes nor stores.
options.explanation: Insulin comes only from pancreatic beta cells; in fasting, the liver responds to glucagon by breaking down glycogen and releasing glucose into the blood.

options.label: E
options.text: Adipocytes convert stored triglycerides directly into glucose
options.misconception: Fat tissue is being credited with a conversion it cannot perform.
options.explanation: Fasting glucose comes first from hepatic glycogen breakdown under glucagon; adipose tissue supplies fatty acids as alternative fuel, not direct glucose.

context: Learning objective: contrast the two islet glucose hormones. High glucose → beta-cell insulin → cellular uptake and storage. Low glucose → alpha-cell glucagon (~20% of islet) → hepatic glycogen breakdown and glucose release into blood.
imageCaption: Insulin (fed, storage) vs glucagon (fast, mobilization/ketogenesis); type 1 = beta-cell loss.
